headings.text: Will robots take my job? What Anthropic found
Why robots are not taking these jobs yet
Which jobs robots could do first
What this means if you work with your hands

paragraphs.text: Robots can do 74 percent of physical work tasks but are cheaper than a person for 0.3 percent. Which jobs robots could take first, and how long it would take.

Probably not soon. Anthropic's new robotics study, published on 30 September 2026, found that robots can already do 74 percent of physical work tasks in the US, but are cheaper than a person for only 0.3 percent of them. At the historical rate robots get cheaper, it takes about 40 years for that share to reach 10 percent.
The gap between those two numbers, what robots can do and what is worth paying a robot to do, is the whole story.

The paper, What work can robots do? by Russell Legate-Yang and Maxim Massenkoff, took the roughly 19,000 tasks in the US government's O*NET job database and picked out the physical ones. For each, Claude searched for real robots already doing that kind of work and rated the task by the hardest setting a robot has been shown to handle it in:

A task scores higher the messier the place a robot can already do it. Each occupation then gets an index from 0 to 3, weighted by how much of the working day each task takes. Anthropic published the full data for 923 occupations.
The fastest scenario assumes robot costs fall up to four times faster than they historically have, and robots learn new tasks twice as quickly. Even then, it takes until 2050.
The study lists what stands in the way, task by task:
The highest scoring occupations are almost all driving and heavy equipment work, where robots already operate in real settings:

Only three of 923 occupations score above 2, and 264, more than a quarter, score zero. The study also found that workers in the most exposed jobs earn about 30 dollars an hour less and are far less likely to hold a degree.

Robot capability is moving, but the economics are not close for most physical work, and they move slowly. A delivery driver faces a real but distant risk, since self driving vehicles already operate in some cities. An electrician or a nurse faces almost none from robots.

Our index scores AI displacement risk from published research, and today drivers sit low on it: Taxi Drivers (25) and Heavy and Tractor-Trailer Truck Drivers (19). That is because the research it draws on is mostly about language AI, which barely touches driving. AI vs robots explains why the two point at almost completely different jobs, and jobs safe from both lists the occupations neither reaches.
